pathway.title: Compass Minerals International Inc — Full credit assessment
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: - Revenue is steady in demand but volatile in volume, which makes earnings lumpy rather than fragile. Highway deicing volumes rose 20.41% in fiscal 2025 and fell 2.54% in the nine months to June 2026 while the average highway price rose 7.80%, and prices reset only at annual tenders, so a mild winter cuts volume at once and price can recover only a year later. Creditors should underwrite the average of several winters, not the latest. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-09-30_cmp.htm.jsonl, page 12; calculation F4

- Margins depend on freight and mine costs, which management has not yet brought down. Shipping and handling cost is 27.60% of sales and the company says mine-level costs are improving but not at the pace expected, so price increases in the salt segment can be absorbed by cost before they reach cash flow. The adjusted EBITDA margin was 18.05% over the last twelve months against 15.98% in fiscal 2025. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); EX99.1_2026-06-30_cmp_cmp-q32026earningsreleasee-htm.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation F4

- Cash conversion is adequate but helped by working capital. Free cash flow was USD 77.9 million over the last twelve months, 0.33x adjusted EBITDA, after negative USD 99.8 million in fiscal 2024 and USD 128.0 million in fiscal 2025 when an inventory release of USD 87.3 million helped, so conversion depends on the winter cycle and capital spending, which management is holding to a guided range. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation F5

- Leverage is moderate and falling but rests on adjusted earnings. Net debt is USD 660.3 million, which is 2.83x adjusted EBITDA and 3.05x reported EBITDA, and the interest burden is high because the 8.00% notes cost about USD 52.0 million a year in cash, so interest cover on expense of 3.19x leaves limited room for an earnings miss. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation F1; calculation F3; calculation F6

- Liquidity and refinancing are adequate near term and concentrated later. Liquidity of USD 328.1 million covers the revolver draw of USD 35.0 million, no principal falls due in fiscal 2026 or 2027, and the revolver is due in May 2028, but 89.29% of principal is a single 2030 bond that is callable at 104.0% from July 2027, so refinancing capacity depends on market access in 2027 and 2028. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-09-30_cmp.htm.jsonl, page 176; calculation F9

- Governance and financial policy support creditors but are untested. There is no sponsor, dividends have been suspended since April 2024, and asset sales and cash retired the 2027 notes, but control weaknesses remain and every listed executive officer took the current post in the last three years, so a new weakness would be hard to detect early. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0)

- The primary downside is a mild winter that coincides with cost inflation and a working-capital build. A fiscal 2024-type winter would cut highway volumes by 16.95% against fiscal 2025, and a repeat of fiscal 2024 free cash flow would use about 30.42% of today's liquidity, so the issuer has room to absorb one such year but not two in a row. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-09-30_cmp.htm.jsonl, page 125; calculation F7

runs.text: Strengths. The first strength is a low-cost, high-scale salt franchise. The Goderich mine is described as the largest underground rock salt mine in the world, with a deep-water port, and the company has logistics depots close to its customers, so delivered cost is competitive in a product where freight is a large part of price; this lowers the risk of losing tenders and supports volume through weak winters. The second strength is near-term refinancing safety: no principal falls due before May 2028 and liquidity is USD 328.1 million, so a poor quarter can be absorbed without a financing event. The third is financial policy: dividends are suspended and disposal proceeds and cash retired the 2027 notes, so cash accrues to debt reduction. The fourth is a Plant Nutrition segment that has turned from a USD 86.4 million operating loss in fiscal 2024 to USD 20.8 million of operating income in the nine months to June 2026, which diversifies earnings away from weather. The fifth is an improving earnings base: adjusted EBITDA rose to USD 233.2 million over the last twelve months. Basis: 10-K_2025-09-30_cmp.htm.jsonl, pages 9–13; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation F10

Weaknesses. The first weakness is weather dependence with an annual price cycle, so volume shocks hit earnings at once and price offsets arrive late. The second is concentration: Goderich produced 50.29% of fiscal 2025 salt tonnage, so a single-site disruption would remove about half of salt output. The third is interest burden: the 8.00% notes cost about USD 52.0 million a year, and cover on interest expense is 3.19x, so cost or volume misses have a fast effect on cash flow after interest. The fourth is a single large maturity, with 89.29% of principal due in 2030, which makes refinancing access in 2027 and 2028 the key test. The fifth is governance and reporting quality, with unremediated control weaknesses and a new management team, which raises the risk that figures or execution disappoint. Basis: 10-K_2025-09-30_cmp.htm.jsonl, page 12; Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation F3; calculation F6; calculation F9

blocks.title: Transaction summary and new debt issues

runs.text: No new debt issue or acquisition is reported after June 30, 2026 in the documents read. The transactions that shape the creditor position are all earlier. On June 16, 2025 the company issued USD 650.0 million of 8.00% senior unsecured notes due 2030 and used the proceeds to repay the revolver and term loan in full and to redeem USD 350.0 million of its 6.75% notes due 2027; the same day a fifth amendment fixed revolver commitments at USD 325.0 million and reset the financial covenants to a first lien leverage test and an interest coverage test. On March 30, 2026 it redeemed the remaining USD 150.0 million of the 2027 notes at par from cash, and on March 19, 2026 it extended its receivables financing facility to March 2029. On March 1, 2026 it sold the Wynyard sulfate of potash business for total consideration of about USD 30.8 million, receiving USD 23.3 million of net cash and booking a USD 14.5 million loss, of which USD 13.1 million is non-cash. In 2025 it exited the Fortress fire retardant business it had bought in 2023, selling the assets for USD 20.0 million, and in January 2024 it ended its lithium project after an impairment of USD 74.8 million. For creditors, the sequence moved the company from secured bank debt and subordinated notes to a structure dominated by one unsecured bond due 2030, with a small revolver and receivables facility, removed near-term maturities and stopped capital going to projects outside salt and sulfate of potash. Basis: 10-Q_2026-06-30_cmp.htm.jsonl, pages 8–11; 10-Q_2026-06-30_cmp.htm.jsonl, pages 13–15; 10-K_2025-09-30_cmp.htm.jsonl, pages 176–178; 10-K_2024-09-30_cmp.htm.jsonl, page 156; calculation B12; calculation B13; calculation B14

fields.value: Leverage on the company's own debt definition fell in two steps. Total debt, which is long-term debt net of financing costs and excludes finance leases, went from USD 917.5 million at September 30, 2024 to USD 832.2 million a year later and USD 716.6 million at June 30, 2026, while last-twelve-month reported EBITDA moved from negative USD 13.7 million in fiscal 2024 to USD 118.0 million in fiscal 2025 and USD 216.6 million. Reported EBITDA carries non-cash charges, USD 191.0 million of impairments in fiscal 2024 and USD 53.7 million in fiscal 2025, so reported leverage is not calculable for fiscal 2024 and is 7.05x for fiscal 2025. Taking only the fiscal 2025 impairment out of EBITDA would give 4.85x, so about 2.20x of the 3.74x fall to 3.31x is that charge leaving the base, and the rest is debt paydown and earnings growth. On the issuer-adjusted measure, which adds the charges back, gross leverage was 4.45x, 4.19x and 3.07x and net leverage at June 30, 2026 is 2.83x, matching the company's own 2.8x. Creditors should therefore anchor on adjusted leverage near 3x and reported leverage near 3.3x, and treat any reading of a seven-turn improvement as an artefact of the base year.

fields.value: The strongest case against caution is that the company's own measures are consistent and improving. Adjusted EBITDA rose to USD 233.2 million over the last twelve months from USD 198.8 million in fiscal 2025, net leverage is 2.83x, S&P is reported by the company to have raised the rating to B+, and fiscal 2026 guidance of USD 218 million to USD 242 million (midpoint USD 230 million) implies earnings hold near the last-twelve-month level while the nearest maturity is 22 months away. That case wins if net leverage stays near 3x at the December 31, 2026 balance sheet, when working capital is at its seasonal high, and if cover on interest expense holds near 3.19x once two coupons fall in one twelve-month window. Caution wins if adjusted EBITDA slips below the guidance midpoint, if cash add-backs recur (restructuring of USD 4.3 million and recall costs of USD 2.1 million in fiscal 2025), or if revolver borrowings rise above USD 35.0 million at a seasonal low.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Compass Minerals is a weather-exposed producer that depends on one large mine and a largely new management team, with no controlling sponsor behind it, so creditors rely on operating delivery and cash discipline, not owner support.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Salt supplies about 82% of sales, and the Goderich mine alone produced about half of the salt tonnage in fiscal 2025. Financial policy has been aligned with creditors since April 2024: no dividends, and disposal proceeds used with cash to retire debt. Governance remains the weak point, with unremediated control weaknesses and a new operations chief in August 2026, so sponsor and governance risk is Medium.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Earnings follow winter weather, so volumes swing before prices can respond. Highway deicing volumes rose 20.41% in fiscal 2025 on a more normal winter and fell 2.54% in the nine months to June 2026, while the average highway price rose 7.80%. Highway sales are won mostly in annual government tenders, so a mild winter cuts volume at once and price can only recover at the next bid, which is why one winter's results should not be read as the run rate.

Goderich produced 50.29% of fiscal 2025 salt tonnage, nearly half of the workforce is under collective agreements, and a new three-year Goderich agreement was announced in May 2026, which removes the nearest labour deadline at that site.

Segment operating income was USD 20.8 million in the nine months to June 2026 against USD 0.3 million a year earlier and an operating loss of USD 86.4 million in fiscal 2024, so the segment now supports cash flow instead of draining it, though one site at Ogden now provides all its capacity.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Governance is the weak point because reporting quality has not yet been re-established. Material weaknesses first reported with a restatement are still being remediated, the auditor gave an adverse opinion on internal control at both year ends, every listed executive officer took the current post between January 2024 and September 2025, and one has already left, so creditors lean on figures and a team without a long record.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Transactions since 2024 are repair, not expansion. Management ended the lithium project, exited Fortress (sold for USD 20.0 million), refinanced with USD 650.0 million of notes, sold Wynyard for cash proceeds of USD 23.3 million and redeemed the last USD 150.0 million of 2027 notes, which shows creditor-aligned priorities but also a record of capital lost on projects outside the core.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: - Unit cost is the lever management has not yet delivered. Shipping and handling cost is 27.60% of fiscal 2025 sales, management says mine-level costs are improving but not at the pace it expected, and it expects production costs to stay elevated, so the pricing gains in the salt segment can be consumed by cost before they reach creditors.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The strongest evidence against caution is that, in management's words, salt has no known cost-effective alternative for most high-volume uses, that no customer reached 10% of sales in any of the last three fiscal years, that highway prices rose 7.80% in the nine months to June 2026 and management describes the coming highway bid season as constructive, and that Plant Nutrition earnings have recovered. Management also reports a stronger-than-average winter in fiscal 2026. These support a view that the business is steadier than its weather exposure suggests. The view would improve if the next winter is average and the fiscal 2027 volume decline management expects is mild, if remediation of the control weaknesses is reported complete, and if Goderich production costs fall. It would worsen if a mine or labour disruption hits Goderich, if the tariffs announced for August 2026 reach Canadian salt exports, or if the board reverses the dividend suspension before debt is lower.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: No new debt issue or acquisition is reported after June 30, 2026 in the documents read. The transactions that shape the creditor position are all earlier. On June 16, 2025 the company issued USD 650.0 million of 8.00% senior unsecured notes due 2030 and used the proceeds to repay the revolver and term loan in full and to redeem USD 350.0 million of its 6.75% notes due 2027; the same day a fifth amendment fixed revolver commitments at USD 325.0 million and reset the financial covenants to a first lien leverage test and an interest coverage test. On March 30, 2026 it redeemed the remaining USD 150.0 million of the 2027 notes at par from cash, and on March 19, 2026 it extended its receivables financing facility to March 2029. On March 1, 2026 it sold the Wynyard sulfate of potash business for total consideration of about USD 30.8 million, receiving USD 23.3 million of net cash and booking a USD 14.5 million loss, of which USD 13.1 million is non-cash. In 2025 it exited the Fortress fire retardant business it had bought in 2023, selling the assets for USD 20.0 million, and in January 2024 it ended its lithium project after an impairment of USD 74.8 million. For creditors, the sequence moved the company from secured bank debt and subordinated notes to a structure dominated by one unsecured bond due 2030, with a small revolver and receivables facility, removed near-term maturities and stopped capital going to projects outside salt and sulfate of potash.

fields.value: Overall, Compass Minerals presents Medium sponsor and governance risk. The key supported behaviour is the suspension of dividends in April 2024 and the use of asset-sale proceeds and cash to retire notes, which matters because it keeps cash in the business and lowers refinancing exposure, and implies a financial policy aligned with creditors. Countervailing evidence is the unremediated control weaknesses, a restatement, a notice of default in September 2024 for a late quarterly report that was cured, and a management team in which every listed officer took the current post since January 2024. Further analysis requires the proxy statement, the executed credit agreement and indenture, and the fiscal 2026 annual report. The review is complete with limitations at a Medium risk level.

fields.value: The strongest evidence against calling the profile fragile is that adjusted EBITDA rose to USD 233.2 million over the last twelve months, that the company reports first lien net leverage of about 0.01x at September 30, 2025 against a covenant maximum that was 2.75x then and is 2.50x now, that S&P is reported to have raised the rating to B+ with adjusted leverage of 3.1x, that management describes the coming highway bid season as constructive, and that guidance of USD 218 million to USD 242 million implies earnings hold near the current level. These points make a stable view plausible. The view would improve if net leverage on reported EBITDA stays at or below 3.05x at the December 31, 2026 balance sheet, when working capital peaks, if remediation of the control weaknesses is reported complete, and if the revolver is extended before May 2027. It would worsen if the fiscal 2026 fourth quarter falls below the guidance midpoint implied for it, if revolver borrowings rise above USD 35.0 million at a seasonal low, or if Goderich output is interrupted.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths. The first strength is a low-cost, high-scale salt franchise. The Goderich mine is described as the largest underground rock salt mine in the world, with a deep-water port, and the company has logistics depots close to its customers, so delivered cost is competitive in a product where freight is a large part of price; this lowers the risk of losing tenders and supports volume through weak winters. The second strength is near-term refinancing safety: no principal falls due before May 2028 and liquidity is USD 328.1 million, so a poor quarter can be absorbed without a financing event. The third is financial policy: dividends are suspended and disposal proceeds and cash retired the 2027 notes, so cash accrues to debt reduction. The fourth is a Plant Nutrition segment that has turned from a USD 86.4 million operating loss in fiscal 2024 to USD 20.8 million of operating income in the nine months to June 2026, which diversifies earnings away from weather. The fifth is an improving earnings base: adjusted EBITDA rose to USD 233.2 million over the last twelve months.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Weaknesses. The first weakness is weather dependence with an annual price cycle, so volume shocks hit earnings at once and price offsets arrive late. The second is concentration: Goderich produced 50.29% of fiscal 2025 salt tonnage, so a single-site disruption would remove about half of salt output. The third is interest burden: the 8.00% notes cost about USD 52.0 million a year, and cover on interest expense is 3.19x, so cost or volume misses have a fast effect on cash flow after interest. The fourth is a single large maturity, with 89.29% of principal due in 2030, which makes refinancing access in 2027 and 2028 the key test. The fifth is governance and reporting quality, with unremediated control weaknesses and a new management team, which raises the risk that figures or execution disappoint.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Compass Minerals produces rock salt, evaporated salt and magnesium chloride for road deicing, consumer and industrial uses, and sulfate of potash fertilizer, operating mines in Ontario, Louisiana and Cheshire and a solar evaporation plant in Utah. Salt is about 82% of sales, and highway deicing alone is about 63% of Salt segment sales, sold mostly through annual government tenders. The credit link is that demand for salt has no known cost-effective substitute for most high-volume uses, which gives cash-flow visibility on volumes in an average winter, but the same sales are weather-driven and seasonal, with salt earnings concentrated in the December and March quarters and cash flow in the first half of the calendar year, so liquidity preservation and the revolver matter more than annual averages. The company exited a fire retardant acquisition in 2025, ended a lithium project in January 2024 and sold its Wynyard sulfate of potash plant in March 2026, so the business that remains is narrower and more focused than it was three years ago.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Compass Minerals International, Inc. is a Delaware holding company whose subsidiaries conduct all operations, so creditors of the parent notes depend on subsidiary cash flows and on guarantees from certain unnamed domestic subsidiaries; the revolver is secured on substantially all U.S. assets, the Goderich mine and stock of certain subsidiaries, and the receivables facility sits in a separate special purpose subsidiary whose assets are not available to other creditors. There is no sponsor or controlling shareholder in the filings; Koch held about 17% after its 2022 placement, with the current holding not supplied. The credit implication is that distribution and exit pressure from an owner is absent, but so is a committed source of equity support, and structural priority between the secured revolver, the receivables facility and the unsecured notes cannot be fully read without the executed documents.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Revenue follows volume times price. Highway volumes depend on snowfall and are sold through annual tenders and some multi-year contracts, with about 75% of UK highway customers on multi-year contracts, so price is set once a year while volume is known only after the winter; consumer and industrial salt, 37% of Salt segment sales, is steadier and higher priced. No customer or affiliated group exceeded 10% of sales in the last three fiscal years. Plant Nutrition sells sulfate of potash, which commands a premium to muriate of potash, mostly to U.S. customers (88%), and its average price rose 10.16% in the nine months to June 2026. The revenue is therefore predictable in direction but cyclical in size, exposed to weather and, for sulfate of potash, to imports and commodity potash; the creditor consequence is that one winter's revenue is a poor guide to coverage and the prudent reading uses a multi-year average.

fields.name: Quote

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Costs are dominated by product cost (57.07% of fiscal 2025 sales) and shipping and handling (27.60%), with selling, general and administrative cost at 9.11% after a reduction of USD 24.5 million in fiscal 2025. Mining and processing carry a large fixed element and are energy-intensive (electricity, diesel and natural gas), freight depends on distance and fuel, and about half of the workforce is unionised, so operating leverage is high: lower volume raises cost per ton, and inflation in freight or labour is hard to offset until the next tender. Management expects production costs to stay elevated near term and says mine-level costs have not yet improved at the pace expected. Margins can be defended against modest cost inflation through pricing gains, as the 7.80% highway price rise shows, but not against a combined volume and cost shock, so creditors should treat the 18.05% adjusted EBITDA margin as a good-winter margin.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Capital expenditure was USD 114.2 million in fiscal 2024, USD 69.7 million in fiscal 2025 and USD 62.1 million in the nine months to June 2026, with fiscal 2026 guidance of USD 90 million to USD 110 million; no split between maintenance and growth is stated, so flexibility cannot be measured. Cash interest paid was USD 59.3 million in fiscal 2025 and USD 41.6 million over the last twelve months, cash taxes were USD 38.5 million over the last twelve months, and working capital swings with inventory, which released USD 87.3 million in fiscal 2025. The result is that free cash flow of USD 77.9 million over the last twelve months is about 0.33x adjusted EBITDA, enough to repay debt gradually but not to retire the 2030 notes, which means refinancing will be needed. Capital spending can be cut as it was in fiscal 2025 (down 39.0%), which gives some protection in a downside, but cuts that defer mine maintenance would raise cost later.

fields.name: Quote

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Competitive rivalry is strong: salt is a commodity, competitors in North America include large nationally recognised companies and regional producers, and two competitors serve the UK highway market, so price competes within delivered cost and the company's depots, Great Lakes position and deep-water port are its edge; creditors should expect price gains to be contested. Entry barriers differ: the filing says they are low in consumer and industrial salt, and, as an analyst reading rather than a company statement, they are high for rock salt mining because few mines combine scale and port access. Substitutes are weak for high-volume uses by management's account, and for sulfate of potash the substitute is muriate of potash, which is cheaper but contains chloride. Buyer power is high in highway deicing because government buyers tender annually, and low in sulfate of potash where the company is the only North American producer. Supplier power matters through energy, freight and, for some products, purchased potassium chloride and calcium chloride, with natural gas partly hedged. The net effect on credit is that pricing power is moderate and cost pass-through slow, which supports the view of volatile but recoverable margins.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Only three factors change credit outcomes. Political and regulatory: U.S. tariffs of up to 50% on certain Canadian imports were announced for August 19, 2026, and Canadian mines supply U.S. highway customers, but the company reports its products are compliant with the United States-Mexico-Canada trade agreement and its Canadian exports were previously exempt, so the effect is not quantified and could affect Goderich margins; Utah rule-making on the Great Salt Lake may affect extraction at Ogden, which underpins sulfate of potash and solar salt output. Economic: freight, fuel and labour inflation and interest rates bear on cost and on the revolver rate of about 5.8%. Social and technological factors are not credit drivers on the filings read. The consequence is that the Canadian tariff outcome and Ogden's lake access are monitoring items, not conclusions.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths: scale and port-linked logistics at Goderich, near-term maturity clearance, aligned financial policy, Plant Nutrition recovery and a rating upgrade, each supporting debt service. Weaknesses: weather dependence, mine concentration, interest burden, single 2030 maturity and weak reporting controls, each constraining cash flow or visibility. Opportunities that could improve credit quality: pricing momentum in highway bids, further debt reduction from free cash flow, refinancing the 2030 notes after the first call date at a lower coupon, and mine efficiency gains that management has not yet delivered. Threats that could weaken credit quality: a mild winter, freight and labour inflation, tariffs on Canadian exports, loss of Goderich output, a change in dividend policy and a failure to remediate control weaknesses.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Business scale and market position are average: the company leads in North American sulfate of potash and operates the largest underground salt mine in the world, but sells commodities and has USD 1,292.1 million of last-twelve-month revenue. Competitive advantage is average: logistics and asset quality help, but there is little differentiation. Diversification is weak: two product families, one mine for about half of salt tons and weather exposure dominate. Cost and capex flexibility is average: spending has been cut but costs are largely fixed and logistics-driven. Margin stability is weak to average: the adjusted EBITDA margin moved from 18.46% in fiscal 2024 to 15.98% in fiscal 2025 and 18.05% over the last twelve months. Free cash flow stability is weak: negative in fiscal 2024, positive since, with seasonal and inventory effects. Ability to refinance is average: a single 2030 bond at a high coupon, no maturity before 2028, and a recent rating upgrade reported by the company. Liquidity is average to strong against near-term obligations but flattered by the seasonal low. Financial policy and governance is average: aligned in behaviour but with weak controls. The credit supports are leverage near 3x, clear maturities and aligned policy; the constraints are volatility, concentration and interest burden; the trend is improving; the missing data are covenant definitions, peers and the fiscal 2026 year end.

Tailwinds are the constructive bid season, Plant Nutrition momentum and lower debt. Headwinds are volume normalisation, cost inflation, tariffs and the 2028 revolver. Over three to five years the issue is refinancing the 2030 notes, callable from July 2027 at 104.0% and at par from July 2029, and keeping leverage low enough to do so; sector demand for salt grows slowly (flat to about 1% a year by management's estimate) while prices have risen about 3% to 4% a year, which supports modest growth only.

fields.value: The scenario replays fiscal 2024, the issuer's own weak-winter year. The initiating condition is a mild 2026-27 winter in which highway volumes fall by about the 16.95% by which fiscal 2024 volumes trailed fiscal 2025, on top of the normalisation management already expects. The first operational break is unabsorbed fixed cost at the mines and unsold salt that raises inventory, as in fiscal 2024 when payables fell and inventory built. The financial transmission is lower Salt earnings and a working-capital build that turned operating cash flow to USD 14.4 million in fiscal 2024 and free cash flow to negative USD 99.8 million; the same result today would use about 30.42% of liquidity of USD 328.1 million, mainly through revolver borrowings. Leverage would rise because debt would not fall and adjusted EBITDA would decline, and the covenant tests and the revolver maturity in May 2028 would become more relevant. Management's levers are capital expenditure, inventory release, suspension of dividends already in place and asset sales. Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress in one such year because liquidity and the maturity profile are stronger than in fiscal 2024, and the observable triggers are revolver borrowings above USD 35.0 million at a seasonal low, a December quarter working-capital build and adjusted EBITDA below the guidance range.

fields.value: Overall, Compass Minerals presents an adequate business profile supported by the scale and port-linked logistics of the Goderich mine, a recovering Plant Nutrition segment and aligned financial policy, but credit quality is constrained by weather dependence, mine concentration and an 8.00% bond that makes interest the heaviest fixed claim. Cash-flow durability appears adequate in an average winter and weak in a mild one, because free cash flow is seasonal and was negative in fiscal 2024. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on leverage staying near 3x and on market access in 2027 and 2028, before the revolver falls due in May 2028. The primary downside path is a mild winter with cost inflation that builds inventory and draws the revolver. Further analysis would require the covenant definitions and compliance certificates, the executed documents, the fiscal 2026 annual report and a peer set. The review is complete with limitations, and the top risk is weather-driven earnings volatility.
